CLIPPER SHIP "ADELAIDE"
The front cover of this menu is a reproduction of an authentic Currier & Ives clipper ship print.
Currier & Ives, known as the "Printmakers of America", graphically preserved the glorious clipper
ship era in a magnificent series of clipper ship prints. This print, one of a series, is being reproduced
through the courtesy of The Mariners Museum, Newport News, Virginia.
The full development of the fast-moving clipper ships coincided remarkably with the glittering
discovery of gold in America and faraway Australia. Clipper ships sailed forward in a dizzy attempt
to combine record breaking speeds with cargo carrying capacity. Never before, nor since, has the
world seen anything like the sensational years that followed the Gold Rush. The clipper ship
"Adelaide" was built in response to the demand for speed and to accommodate the relentless surge
of gold-seekers. Built by A. C. Bell in 1854 in New York, she had a knife-sharp bow, long narrow
hull and magnificent display of canvas. Her speed and maneuverability, as she tore around the
Horn, was prodigious. Right up to the beginning of the Civil War, which disrupted the trade routes
of the "Adelaide," she brought unprecedented prosperity to her East coast owners. Though her glory
was brief, the adventures of the "Adelaide" still capture the imagination of those who love the sea.
Like Pan Am's modern Clippers* of the air, the early clipper ships traveled the lanes of com-
merce to all the far places of the world... to Japan... to Australia... and, in the days of the
great gold rush, from America's east coast, around Cape Horn, South America, to California.
Our current equipment... the Clipper fleet of the Twentieth Century... consists of the finest
commercial aircraft ever developedaircraft that have helped us establish an unparalleled record
for safety, speed and service.
